description: Small Poznań team of CS students (Python/C++), with a maths grad student likely joining. We'll pick a challenge after the full statements drop on October 28 — we want something interactive and visual, built on real NASA data. Looking for 1–2 more: front-end/UI, data visualization or design.
summary:
Lunar OPS is an open-source web app that helps choose a lunar south pole landing site by showing where and when a lander has both the Sun and the Earth in view. At the pole the Sun stays near the horizon, so terrain blocks sunlight and Earth visibility, and a site that works today may fail in two weeks.

We combine the NASA LOLA 5 m digital elevation model, which gives the real horizon of each candidate site, with JPL Horizons Sun and Earth directions every 10 minutes. A body counts as visible when it is above the local horizon. For each site and date the app reports hours of potential sunlight, geometric Earth visibility, windows when both are available, and a countdown to sunset and Earthset. Users can compare two scenarios side by side, shift the mission start date, and explore a 3D terrain view with shadows from the real Sun direction.

We cross-checked Sun and Earth directions against an independent skyfield DE440s implementation (within 0.001°) and computed the horizon with two independent implementations. The tool models geometric visibility only, not radio link budget.

Code: github.com/ohiiartem/lunar-ops
details:
What it does. Lunar OPS compares candidate landing sites and dates at the lunar south pole. For each scenario it reports hours of potential sunlight, geometric Earth visibility, windows when both are available, and a countdown to sunset and Earthset. Scenarios can be compared side by side, and the mission start date can be shifted.

How it works. NASA LOLA 5 m DEM tiles (16 x 16 km per site) give the real horizon in every direction. JPL Horizons gives Sun and Earth directions every 10 minutes. A body is visible when it is above the local horizon. A 3D terrain view shows shadows from the real Sun direction.

Tools. Python (FastAPI, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj) for the backend; TypeScript, Three.js and Vite for the web app. skyfield (DE440s) was used only to cross-check our Sun and Earth directions (within 0.001°).

Factors considered. Terrain curvature in the horizon calculation, 10-minute time resolution, and the fact that about 90% of the polar DEM pixels are interpolated. We model geometric visibility only, not radio link budget.

Impact. Mission planners can quickly see how site choice and date change power and communication opportunities. The project is open source: github.com/ohiiartem/lunar-ops
dataRefs: NASA LOLA 5 m/pixel DEM (PGDA LOLA_5mpp archive)
NASA JPL Horizons System (Sun and Earth directions)
NASA JPL DE440s planetary ephemeris (cross-check with skyfield)
